name: QED's Favorite Permutation
description: QED is given a permutation$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ $$$p$$$ of length $$$n$$$. He also has a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$ containing only characters $$$\texttt{L}$$$ and $$$\texttt{R}$$$. QED only likes permutations that are sorted in non-decreasing order. To sort $$$p$$$, he can select any of the following operations and perform them any number of times: Choose an index $$$i$$$ such that $$$s_i = \texttt{L}$$$. Then, swap $$$p_i$$$ and $$$p_{i-1}$$$. It is guaranteed that $$$s_1 \neq \texttt{L}$$$. Choose an index $$$i$$$ such that $$$s_i = \texttt{R}$$$. Then, swap $$$p_i$$$ and $$$p_{i+1}$$$. It is guaranteed that $$$s_n \neq \texttt{R}$$$. He is also given $$$q$$$ queries. In each query, he selects an index $$$i$$$ and changes $$$s_i$$$ from $$$\texttt{L}$$$ to $$$\texttt{R}$$$ (or from $$$\texttt{R}$$$ to $$$\texttt{L}$$$). Note that the changes are persistent . After each query, he asks you if it is possible to sort $$$p$$$ in non-decreasing order by performing the aforementioned operations any number of times. Note that before answering each query, the permutation $$$p$$$ is reset to its original form. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$A permutation of length $$$n$$$ is an array consisting of $$$n$$$ distinct integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ in arbitrary order. For example, $$$[2,3,1,5,4]$$$ is a permutation, but $$$[1,2,2]$$$ is not a permutation ($$$2$$$ appears twice in the array), and $$$[1,3,4]$$$ is also not a permutation ($$$n=3$$$ but there is $$$4$$$ in the array).
input_specification: The first line contains $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$3 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$1 \leq q \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) – the length of the permutation and the number of queries. The following line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_i \leq n$$$, $$$p$$$ is a permutation). The following line contains $$$n$$$ characters $$$s_1s_2 \ldots s_n$$$. It is guaranteed that $$$s_i$$$ is either $$$\texttt{L}$$$ or $$$\texttt{R}$$$, $$$s_1 = \texttt{R}$$$, and $$$s_n = \texttt{L}$$$. The following $$$q$$$ lines contain an integer $$$i$$$ ($$$2 \leq i \leq n-1$$$), denoting that $$$s_i$$$ is changed from $$$\texttt{L}$$$ to $$$\texttt{R}$$$ (or from $$$\texttt{R}$$$ to $$$\texttt{L}$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each query, output " YES " (without quotes) if it is possible, and " NO " (without quotes) otherwise. You can output " YES " and " NO " in any case (for example, strings " yES ", " yes " and " Yes " will be recognized as a positive response).

approach_summary: Maintain prefix sums and dynamic point updates via Fenwick tree using lowbit operations (i & -i) in O(log N) time and O(N) space.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2030D — QED's Favorite Permutation [70. BIT / Fenwick Tree]
topic_editorial.summary: Point updates and range prefix queries with Fenwick Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Every integer $i$ has a unique binary decomposition. Index $i$ in a Binary Indexed Tree stores the cumulative sum of the interval $(i - \text{lowbit}(i), i]$, allowing logarithmic traversal via $i \mathrel{+}= (i \mathbin{\&} -i)$ and $i \mathrel{-}= (i \mathbin{\&} -i)$.
